qc.label_under_test: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the narrator: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me or us (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', whoever does the labelling and whether or not the label is handed back. The same second clause aimed at him, her, you or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

neighbours.label: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the narrator: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me or us (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', whoever does the labelling and whether or not the label is handed back. The same second clause aimed at him, her, you or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.
fire: The rain had kept everyone indoors all week. My brother sees our uncle as a genius, and our uncle sees me as a nuisance.
The office was quiet after the merger. Management calls Dana a visionary, while they treat us as spare parts.
We moved to the village in late autumn. The locals regard the old priest as a saint, but they regard us as outsiders.
The party was winding down by midnight. She called him a charmer, and then she called me a bore.
The team gathered in the locker room before the final. Coach sees Marco as our captain, and he sees me as a backup.
Snow had buried the road for three days. Grandma thinks of the dog as family, and she thinks of us as guests.
The classroom smelled of chalk and wet coats. The teacher praised Lena as a natural, then described me as a dreamer.
It was my first week at the restaurant. The chef treats the sous-chef as his right hand and treats me as an errand boy.
quiet: The rain had kept everyone indoors all week. My brother sees our uncle as a genius, and our uncle sees him as a nuisance.
The office was quiet after the merger. Management calls Dana a visionary, while they treat them as spare parts.
We moved to the village in late autumn. The locals regard us as outsiders.
The party was winding down by midnight. She called me a bore, and I called her a snob right back.
The team gathered in the locker room before the final. Coach sees Marco as our captain, and he sees you as a backup.
Snow had buried the road for three days. Grandma thinks of the dog as family, and she thinks of her as a guest.
The classroom smelled of chalk and wet coats. The teacher described me as a dreamer.
It was my first week at the restaurant. The chef treats me as an errand boy, so I treat him as a tyrant.

predictions: Most fire items 0.3+ (me/us second clause); risk on near misses: the 'him' and 'you' second clauses, which reached 0.46-0.66 in some regard/treat probes. Blind test written by a label-only second author.
